Ice Freediver Amber Fillary

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We meet a remarkable ice freediver from Cape Town in her pursuit of a world record and what inspired her to go down that path after years of battling with addiction and major depression.

Unique Selling Point:
On 29 February 2020, forty-seven-year-old Amber Fillary from Cape Town plunged into a hole in a frozen lake near Oslo in Norway to break the record for the longest freedive under ice. She swam a distance of 70meters under 34cm of ice, wearing only a bikini (no fins, no weight to keep her down, no wetsuit) and goggles. She beat the record by 20 meters - all for the sake of mental health. Fillary suffers from severe depression and has battled with addictions all her life. Breaking the world record was a psychological achievement for Fillary where her aim was to give others hope who are suffering from similar problems. Her message was simple: “you can achieve anything if you put your mind to it” and ‘never to give up on your dreams.’

Summary:
Technical skills: At high school she received her Western Province swimming school colours and later on became a swimming coach and lifesaver in the UK where she became accustomed to freezing waters during the cold northern winters. She tried scuba diving for a while in Egypt but found the diving and breathing equipment heavy and cumbersome. Freediving was a natural choice for Fillary as she soon proved to have huge capacity for breath hold and staying calm under water. In 2015 Fillary broke three freediving records at the nationals in Port Elizabeth and was awarded her Springbok colours. In 2017 she became the country’s only representative to partake in the under-ice freediving competition in Finland - a sport relatively unknown in South Africa.
“My first attempt in Finland was like a practice run; I did not know what to expect and was totally unprepared for the conditions of swimming under a layer of thick ice in sub-zero temperatures,” she says. But it made her more determined to try again. In 2019, she made another attempt - this time with some training from South African coach, Allen Stubbs - but panicked and got entangled in the safety line she was attached to. She fell back into a dark space and with the help of Stubbs, and serious technical training in the pool here in Cape Town, went back in 2020 ready for the biggest challenge ever - to break the Guinness World Record.



Further information:
Breaking the world record:
The day of the event was memorable; as the petit 5.9 small frame of Fillary crossed the ice towards the plunge hole where a large professional team was waiting to greet her, many thoughts crossed her mind. “ I had this one chance to beat the record, I can’t blow it.’ Safety divers, supervisors, a judge, medical support….were all there and a video team to record the event for Guinness. Fillary beat the 50meter world record by 20 meters and became the new Guinness World record holder for freediving. She swam 70 meters under ice on one breath with no wetsuit, no weights and no fins, wearing only her bikini and goggles.

Personal battles: What drives athletes to attempt a sport in such an extreme environment? For Fillary it has been the result of a rickety road she has been on all her life. She suffers from sever depression, various forms of addiction, eating disorders and has attempted suicide several times. She has been in and out of rehab since her early twenties and has never been able to maintain a steady job for a long time. Since discovering freediving under ice it has given her the mental challenge to keep her on the straight and narrow. “It is the only place where I find peace.” she says

Extreme sport: Freediving under ice is arguably the most extreme sport and most dangerous with only a handful of athletes in the world excelling in this sport. Taking a single breath of air before submerging under a thick layer of ice to delve into the silent world of such beauty where there is no breathing apparatus brings the athlete close to the pain barrier. The body’s short term involuntary response is to ‘gasp’ for air as well as rapid breath to make the heart work harder. But that is not possible as there is no reserve air available to pump more blood to the heart, and if prolonged, will lead to heart failure.
“Fillary has an ability to control her mind like a clock”, says swimming coach Allen Stubbs who has been training her on her technical skills for the last three years. “She is unique in this way that she can hold her breath far longer than other freedivers and still come out with reserve air.”
“Everything starts in my head. If my headspace isn’t right, I can’t do it, says Fillary. Unlike other freedive ice swimmers, who go into a sauna, do breathing meditation, apnoea exercises and lots of visualisations to deal with their stress and fears, Fillary only pauses briefly before inhaling and entering the water. But she is modest about her abilities and contributes her skills to a simple philosophy of the mind being stronger than the body: “‘I have to be in the right headspace or I will not make it,” she says.
Setting her back: After breaking the world record in February last year, Fillary was elated and was already planning the next achievement - beating the men’s record of 76meters (no fins, no weight, no diving suit). Then came Covid-19 and lockdown. Fillary went back into a dark space of suicidal thoughts and addiction. She tried getting help online but nothing lifted the veil of depression. Then Stubbs got her back in the pool in December last year suggesting a rigorous training schedule. This worked, and Fillary was back on track. It has been three months of preparation, both mental and physical, and Fillary was ready for the ultimate challenge - breaking the men’s freestyle under-ice record. But once again she is facing a setback - travel bans and quarantine has waylaid her plans to go to Finland this February.
Stubbs says, based on her performance in the pool and technical skills, she would have easily broke the men’s record if she went.

“This is another setback for me. I have to have a mental challenge. So I am going to try to beat the ‘stepwalking’ record in Egypt later this year, she says. Stepwalking is an breathold swimming pool discipline where the athlete are weighted down walking on the surface of the pool.

Treatment:
The story is more about Fillary’s psychological achievements; what inspired her to go down that path and how it started. Fillary thrives underwater - she feels in control and at peace. The psychological side of an ice freediver drives the style of storytelling where she pushes her physical and psychological limits to the tipping point. Water, space, light, darkness, and light are strong cinematic elements reflected in the visual elements of the story. There is video footage of Fillary’s 2020 Under-ice Freediving record in Norway both above and below; visuals of her failed attempt in 2019 when she got entangled in ropes; plus a selection of photos in action.
Our visuals will include swimming pool technical training; ice training in an ice bath; yoga exercise; running; and cinematic element shots of water, light, darkness, space and loneliness.
Interviews: Amber Fillary - main case study; A psychiatrist (to talk about mental illness and addictions); her coach, Allen Stubbs and a short sound bite of a fellow ice swimmer, Ryan Stramrood - to talk about the extreme sport and Fillary’s rare talent for this environment.

Press Release:



M I N D O V E R I C Y M A T T E R



Amber Under Ice

Depression is a debilitating illness and the therapy that Amber Fillary (49) found in cold water has been a lifesaver. After spending most of her youth in and out of rehabilitation facilities, battling addiction and an eating disorder, Fillary has finally found the one place where she’s able to live in healthy harmony with herself and find mental wholeness – under the ice. Freezing waters beneath thick ice have become her place of peace and the source of fulfilment and achievement as she sets out to break one world record after another. Carte Blanche met Fillary in Cape Town after setting the record for the longest horizontal swim under ice on a single breath wearing just her costume and a pair of goggles. Currently waiting out Germany’s lockdown, she continues training for an underwater breath-hold Guinness World Record attempt in Egypt this coming November, as well as the men’s under-ice record at the end of February next year in Norway.

Producer: Annalise Lubbe | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


Script: Ice Freediver Amber Fillary

Amber Fillary: Ice freediver - I really struggle to live on earth, on land, but when I am in the water I am relaxed, I am calm, and the voices in my head stop. Yeah, it makes me feel good, it makes me feel whole.

LINK: What you have just seen is Fillary swimming in the icy waters of a Norwegian lake - a far cry from the warm swimming pools back in Cape Town.

Up sound: “So when you go out in your dive, no arms at all level out, start with the stroke on the outside...”

V/O Amber Fillary is an extreme athlete and world record holder for the longest swim under ice while holding her breath. Her journey to success was marred by extreme highs and lows, as she battled with depression, addiction and an eating disorder on the way.

Up music

V/O Fillary’s love for water started when she was a little girl. Her earliest memory is of a tidal pool at St James in Cape Town.

Amber Fillary: Ice freediver - Apparently when I was little I would run at St James and jump in the deep end - to my parent’s horror - so I think from a little child I’ve really liked the water.

V/O At school, she excelled at swimming. She was awarded Western Province colours when she was 13.

Masa Kekana: Tell me about the preparation and the compromises you had to make for your swimming career.

Amber Fillary: It’s training twice a day, it's giving up a lot. I only swam up until maybe standard 7, standard 8, and then I started with anorexia and my swimming coach did not want me to swim any more.

Masa Kekana: Let’s talk about your battles with eating disorders. How did that start?

Amber Fillary: There was a lot of competition with the girls and there were a lot of eating disorders. I wasn’t really happy at school and I think in some ways it started as controlling everything. It kind of spun out of control. Like no matter how much weight I lost it just wasn’t sort of enough.

V/O After leaving school, Fillary studied Fine Art, but didn’t finish her degree. Her eating disorder spilt over into alcohol addiction and she spent most of her twenties in and out of rehab. Depression took over and thoughts of suicide haunted her, something she speaks freely about.

LINK: Most athletes who suffer from depression or drug dependency shy away from talking about it openly for fear of ruining their reputation. But not Amber.

Amber Fillary: It's like waking up and it's like you don’t want to be alive, no matter how good everything is around you. It takes things away and ruins opportunities, it ruins friendships.

V/O Fillary lived in England for a while where she attended AA meetings and managed to hold down a job as a lifeguard at a London pool. This was her first experience with ice water.

Amber Fillary: You know it would snow or the water would ice over that’s where I experienced getting into really cold water and learning the benefits of cold water swimming and that it's good for your mental health.

V/O Fillary’s love for water was the one constant factor in her life. Back in South Africa, she tried freediving: a sport that requires strong mental preparation.

Amber Fillary: In order to hold your breath it's such a mental discipline. So I can't have any thoughts of negativity or anything.

V/O Although Fillary did no serious training in freediving, she excelled at it, setting three national records at the championships in Port Elizabeth in 2015. Her next goal was to break the world record for freediving under ice - a hostile environment she was not used to. On her second attempt at a lake in Finland, she lost her direction under the ice and got tangled in the line.

Up music

Amber Fillary: I was really upset. I didn’t handle the situation well. I was devastated.

Link: After two failed attempts, Amber was back in competition mode. This time, she went to Norway to try to break the Guinness World Record in ice freediving.

V/O Fillary had only three months to get ready for the world record. With the help of swimming coach, Allen Stubbs, she embarked on the challenge of her life.

Allen Stubbs; Swimming coach: It is hard enough swimming 50meters underwater with breaststroke, then on top of it she is going to be in freezing water, but that is not the worst of it, she has to blow out half of the air before she goes because otherwise she will be too buoyant to stay under the water.

V/O The next step was getting accustomed to the water reaching sub-zero temperatures. Ice swimmer Ryan Stramrood - an extreme athlete who swam the Ice Mile in Antarctica in -1°C degree water - introduced Fillary to the ice bath.

Link: I am standing next to an ice bath at a fish factory in Cape Town. Sounds strange, right? But this is as close as ice swimmers here will get to practising for this extreme sport.

Up sound: “Cheers! Heaven.” Masa Kekana: “How are you feeling Amber?” Amber Fillary: “I love it.”

Ryan Stramrood - Ice swimmer: So when you jump into these extreme cold situations the mind just implements this pain, panic and fear and those come together extremely quickly to accentuate self doubt and deny you the ability of rational thought. That is why we sit in these ice tubs because you need to understand that process... and how you are going to overcome the different instincts that kick in.

Up sound: World record day

V/O It was the 29th of February last year, the day of the Guinness World Record at a frozen lake in Norway. A video team, a judge, witnesses and safety divers were all on standby.

Amber Fillary: I walked out onto the ice..

Masa Kekana: In your costume?

Amber Fillary: No I had a little poncho over me with my costume underneath, and then amazingly that day, it snowed, so it was perfect!

Up music

Amber Fillary: And then I took a breath of air and dived under. I had absolutely no feeling of water temperature or anything. I was totally in my head and trying to keep it as still as possible. It was like my private journey.

V/O At 47, Fillary set a new Guinness World Record in the female category. She swam 70 meters on one breath under 34cm of ice wearing only her bikini, goggles and a cap.

UP sound - Amber Fillary: “Oh I am so happy. It was successful and a great dive. So I am super, super happy.”

V/O Dr. Sean Gottschalk works with ice swimmers in Cape Town, who claim that cold-water swimming has improved their mental health.

Dr Sean Gottschalk: Medical doctor - A number of these athletes have reported mood disorders like depression and the cold water is well documented to improve people’s moods. When they come out of the water they get an endorphin rush...so immediately after a swim and days and weeks after these swims it improves their mood

Dr Uschenka Padayachey: Psychiatrist - When you have to be in the moment you purely focus on what you are doing and in that moment it actually brings down the anxiety level because you cannot focus on the negativity.

V/O Dr Uschenka Padayachey, a psychiatrist at a Milnerton clinic, says depression is the cause of eating disorders and substance abuse.

Dr Uschenka Padayachey: When you look at eating disorders, substance use, they are all manifestations of the central core so what the individual is trying to do is to restrict their emotions. It is a way of not having to deal with the pain they are feeling and depression is underlying for all of those things.

V/O The right medication has helped Fillary manage the depression, but addiction remains a battle. For now, she has a goal to achieve.

Amber Fillary: My aim is next year in Norway to do 100 meters; but that is maybe a bit ambitious but otherwise at least 90 meters so I can break the current men’s record.
It's not just about achieving the record that I can maybe reach out and through my achievement help other people achieve their dreams that makes me feel a bit more excited.
________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Promo one
When an ice freediver from Cape Town set out to break the Guinness World Record in Norway, it gave her a sense of self-worth after suffering from a life-long battle with alcohol dependency and depression.

Promo two
When a former addict suffering from depression entered a frozen lake in Norway last year, she made up her mind to override all negative thoughts and set a new world record in ice freediving.

Promo three
When she stepped out onto the ice and took her last breath - wearing only a bikini and cap - before she plunged into the freezing waters of a lake in Norway and broke the world record, Fillary said: “I am super happy.”

V/O At school, she excelled at swimming. She was awarded Western Province colours when she was 13. Masa Kekana: Tell me about the preparation and the compromises you had to make for your swimming career. Amber Fillary: It’s training twice a day, it's giving up a lot. I only swam up until maybe standard 7, standard 8, and then I started with anorexia and my swimming coach did not want me to swim any more. Masa Kekana: Let’s talk about your battles with eating disorders. How did that start? Amber Fillary: There was a lot of competition with the girls and there were a lot of eating disorders. I wasn’t really happy at school and I think in some ways it started as controlling everything. It kind of spun out of control. Like no matter how much weight I lost it just wasn’t sort of enough. V/O After leaving school, Fillary studied Fine Art, but didn’t finish her degree. Her eating disorder spilt over into alcohol addiction and she spent most of her twenties in and out of rehab. Depression took over and thoughts of suicide haunted her, something she speaks freely about. LINK: Most athletes who suffer from depression or drug dependency shy away from talking about it openly for fear of ruining their reputation. But not Amber. Amber Fillary: It's like waking up and it's like you don’t want to be alive, no matter how good everything is around you. It takes things away and ruins opportunities, it ruins friendships. V/O Fillary lived in England for a while where she attended AA meetings and managed to hold down a job as a lifeguard at a London pool. This was her first experience with ice water. Amber Fillary: You know it would snow or the water would ice over that’s where I experienced getting into really cold water and learning the benefits of cold water swimming and that it's good for your mental health. V/O Fillary’s love for water was the one constant factor in her life. Back in South Africa, she tried freediving: a sport that requires strong mental preparation. Amber Fillary: In order to hold your breath it's such a mental discipline. So I can't have any thoughts of negativity or anything. V/O Although Fillary did no serious training in freediving, she excelled at it, setting three national records at the championships in Port Elizabeth in 2015. Her next goal was to break the world record for freediving under ice - a hostile environment she was not used to. On her second attempt at a lake in Finland, she lost her direction under the ice and got tangled in the line. Up music Amber Fillary: I was really upset. I didn’t handle the situation well. I was devastated. Link: After two failed attempts, Amber was back in competition mode. This time, she went to Norway to try to break the Guinness World Record in ice freediving. V/O Fillary had only three months to get ready for the world record. With the help of swimming coach, Allen Stubbs, she embarked on the challenge of her life. Allen Stubbs; Swimming coach: It is hard enough swimming 50meters underwater with breaststroke, then on top of it she is going to be in freezing water, but that is not the worst of it, she has to blow out half of the air before she goes because otherwise she will be too buoyant to stay under the water. V/O The next step was getting accustomed to the water reaching sub-zero temperatures. Ice swimmer Ryan Stramrood - an extreme athlete who swam the Ice Mile in Antarctica in -1°C degree water - introduced Fillary to the ice bath. Link: I am standing next to an ice bath at a fish factory in Cape Town. Sounds strange, right? But this is as close as ice swimmers here will get to practising for this extreme sport. Up sound: “Cheers! Heaven.” Masa Kekana: “How are you feeling Amber?” Amber Fillary: “I love it.” Ryan Stramrood - Ice swimmer: So when you jump into these extreme cold situations the mind just implements this pain, panic and fear and those come together extremely quickly to accentuate self doubt and deny you the ability of rational thought. That is why we sit in these ice tubs because you need to understand that process... and how you are going to overcome the different instincts that kick in. Up sound: World record day V/O It was the 29th of February last year, the day of the Guinness World Record at a frozen lake in Norway. A video team, a judge, witnesses and safety divers were all on standby. Amber Fillary: I walked out onto the ice.. Masa Kekana: In your costume? Amber Fillary: No I had a little poncho over me with my costume underneath, and then amazingly that day, it snowed, so it was perfect! Up music Amber Fillary: And then I took a breath of air and dived under. I had absolutely no feeling of water temperature or anything. I was totally in my head and trying to keep it as still as possible. It was like my private journey. V/O At 47, Fillary set a new Guinness World Record in the female category. She swam 70 meters on one breath under 34cm of ice wearing only her bikini, goggles and a cap. UP sound - Amber Fillary: “Oh I am so happy. It was successful and a great dive. So I am super, super happy.” V/O Dr. Sean Gottschalk works with ice swimmers in Cape Town, who claim that cold-water swimming has improved their mental health. Dr Sean Gottschalk: Medical doctor - A number of these athletes have reported mood disorders like depression and the cold water is well documented to improve people’s moods. When they come out of the water they get an endorphin rush...so immediately after a swim and days and weeks after these swims it improves their mood Dr Uschenka Padayachey: Psychiatrist - When you have to be in the moment you purely focus on what you are doing and in that moment it actually brings down the anxiety level because you cannot focus on the negativity. V/O Dr Uschenka Padayachey, a psychiatrist at a Milnerton clinic, says depression is the cause of eating disorders and substance abuse. Dr Uschenka Padayachey: When you look at eating disorders, substance use, they are all manifestations of the central core so what the individual is trying to do is to restrict their emotions. It is a way of not having to deal with the pain they are feeling and depression is underlying for all of those things. V/O The right medication has helped Fillary manage the depression, but addiction remains a battle. For now, she has a goal to achieve. Amber Fillary: My aim is next year in Norway to do 100 meters; but that is maybe a bit ambitious but otherwise at least 90 meters so I can break the current men’s record. It's not just about achieving the record that I can maybe reach out and through my achievement help other people achieve their dreams that makes me feel a bit more excited. ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo one When an ice freediver from Cape Town set out to break the Guinness World Record in Norway, it gave her a sense of self-worth after suffering from a life-long battle with alcohol dependency and depression. Promo two When a former addict suffering from depression entered a frozen lake in Norway last year, she made up her mind to override all negative thoughts and set a new world record in ice freediving. Promo three When she stepped out onto the ice and took her last breath - wearing only a bikini and cap - before she plunged into the freezing waters of a lake in Norway and broke the world record, Fillary said: “I am super happy.” Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Ice Freediver Amber Fillary (5876) Annalise Lubbe 10 March 2021

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We meet a remarkable ice freediver from Cape Town in her pursuit of a world record and what inspired her to go down that path after years of battling with addiction and major depression.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: On 29 February 2020, forty-seven-year-old Amber Fillary from Cape Town plunged into a hole in a frozen lake near Oslo in Norway to break the record for the longest freedive under ice. She swam a distance of 70meters under 34cm of ice, wearing only a bikini (no fins, no weight to keep her down, no wetsuit) and goggles. She beat the record by 20 meters - all for the sake of mental health. Fillary suffers from severe depression and has battled with addictions all her life. Breaking the world record was a psychological achievement for Fillary where her aim was to give others hope who are suffering from similar problems. Her message was simple: “you can achieve anything if you put your mind to it” and ‘never to give up on your dreams.’
metadata.Summary: Technical skills: At high school she received her Western Province swimming school colours and later on became a swimming coach and lifesaver in the UK where she became accustomed to freezing waters during the cold northern winters. She tried scuba diving for a while in Egypt but found the diving and breathing equipment heavy and cumbersome. Freediving was a natural choice for Fillary as she soon proved to have huge capacity for breath hold and staying calm under water. In 2015 Fillary broke three freediving records at the nationals in Port Elizabeth and was awarded her Springbok colours. In 2017 she became the country’s only representative to partake in the under-ice freediving competition in Finland - a sport relatively unknown in South Africa. “My first attempt in Finland was like a practice run; I did not know what to expect and was totally unprepared for the conditions of swimming under a layer of thick ice in sub-zero temperatures,” she says. But it made her more determined to try again. In 2019, she made another attempt - this time with some training from South African coach, Allen Stubbs - but panicked and got entangled in the safety line she was attached to. She fell back into a dark space and with the help of Stubbs, and serious technical training in the pool here in Cape Town, went back in 2020 ready for the biggest challenge ever - to break the Guinness World Record.
metadata.Further information: Breaking the world record: The day of the event was memorable; as the petit 5.9 small frame of Fillary crossed the ice towards the plunge hole where a large professional team was waiting to greet her, many thoughts crossed her mind. “ I had this one chance to beat the record, I can’t blow it.’ Safety divers, supervisors, a judge, medical support….were all there and a video team to record the event for Guinness. Fillary beat the 50meter world record by 20 meters and became the new Guinness World record holder for freediving. She swam 70 meters under ice on one breath with no wetsuit, no weights and no fins, wearing only her bikini and goggles. Personal battles: What drives athletes to attempt a sport in such an extreme environment? For Fillary it has been the result of a rickety road she has been on all her life. She suffers from sever depression, various forms of addiction, eating disorders and has attempted suicide several times. She has been in and out of rehab since her early twenties and has never been able to maintain a steady job for a long time. Since discovering freediving under ice it has given her the mental challenge to keep her on the straight and narrow. “It is the only place where I find peace.” she says Extreme sport: Freediving under ice is arguably the most extreme sport and most dangerous with only a handful of athletes in the world excelling in this sport. Taking a single breath of air before submerging under a thick layer of ice to delve into the silent world of such beauty where there is no breathing apparatus brings the athlete close to the pain barrier. The body’s short term involuntary response is to ‘gasp’ for air as well as rapid breath to make the heart work harder. But that is not possible as there is no reserve air available to pump more blood to the heart, and if prolonged, will lead to heart failure. “Fillary has an ability to control her mind like a clock”, says swimming coach Allen Stubbs who has been training her on her technical skills for the last three years. “She is unique in this way that she can hold her breath far longer than other freedivers and still come out with reserve air.” “Everything starts in my head. If my headspace isn’t right, I can’t do it, says Fillary. Unlike other freedive ice swimmers, who go into a sauna, do breathing meditation, apnoea exercises and lots of visualisations to deal with their stress and fears, Fillary only pauses briefly before inhaling and entering the water. But she is modest about her abilities and contributes her skills to a simple philosophy of the mind being stronger than the body: “‘I have to be in the right headspace or I will not make it,” she says. Setting her back: After breaking the world record in February last year, Fillary was elated and was already planning the next achievement - beating the men’s record of 76meters (no fins, no weight, no diving suit). Then came Covid-19 and lockdown. Fillary went back into a dark space of suicidal thoughts and addiction. She tried getting help online but nothing lifted the veil of depression. Then Stubbs got her back in the pool in December last year suggesting a rigorous training schedule. This worked, and Fillary was back on track. It has been three months of preparation, both mental and physical, and Fillary was ready for the ultimate challenge - breaking the men’s freestyle under-ice record. But once again she is facing a setback - travel bans and quarantine has waylaid her plans to go to Finland this February. Stubbs says, based on her performance in the pool and technical skills, she would have easily broke the men’s record if she went. “This is another setback for me. I have to have a mental challenge. So I am going to try to beat the ‘stepwalking’ record in Egypt later this year, she says. Stepwalking is an breathold swimming pool discipline where the athlete are weighted down walking on the surface of the pool. Treatment: The story is more about Fillary’s psychological achievements; what inspired her to go down that path and how it started. Fillary thrives underwater - she feels in control and at peace. The psychological side of an ice freediver drives the style of storytelling where she pushes her physical and psychological limits to the tipping point. Water, space, light, darkness, and light are strong cinematic elements reflected in the visual elements of the story. There is video footage of Fillary’s 2020 Under-ice Freediving record in Norway both above and below; visuals of her failed attempt in 2019 when she got entangled in ropes; plus a selection of photos in action. Our visuals will include swimming pool technical training; ice training in an ice bath; yoga exercise; running; and cinematic element shots of water, light, darkness, space and loneliness. Interviews: Amber Fillary - main case study; A psychiatrist (to talk about mental illness and addictions); her coach, Allen Stubbs and a short sound bite of a fellow ice swimmer, Ryan Stramrood - to talk about the extreme sport and Fillary’s rare talent for this environment.
